word:hebrew:H1014.explanation: Gamul is a Hebrew proper name, rendered “Gamul.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. This word occurs twice in the Hebrew corpus, both occurrences appearing in Jeremiah 48:23. Because no short definition or surrounding verse text is available here, the safest understanding is its role as a name. Its precise reference and significance must be determined from the surrounding passage rather than from the name alone.

word:hebrew:H1058.explanation: Bakah means to weep or mourn.

word:hebrew:H1199.explanation: Baara is a personal name, identifying a woman named in the Hebrew Old Testament. It appears once, in 1 Chronicles 8:8, within a genealogy. Because the available wording preserves the name rather than giving an explicit definition, its ordinary meaning is the person it identifies, not a stated quality or action. The surrounding genealogy places Baara among family relationships and records of descent.

word:hebrew:H1256.explanation: Beraiah is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or common object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this name appears once, at 1 Chronicles 8:21. The available rendering preserves it as “Beraiah,” so the evidence supports recognizing it as a proper name, not assigning it an additional ordinary-word meaning. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain this person’s role in that passage.

word:hebrew:H127.explanation: Adamah means soil or ground; it can also refer to the earth or a land.

word:hebrew:H1384.explanation: This Hebrew word describes a person who is “crookbackt,” meaning someone whose back is bent or hunched. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Leviticus 21:20. The word identifies a physical condition rather than an action, feeling, or character trait. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning points to a visibly curved back or bodily deformity.

word:hebrew:H1410.explanation: This Hebrew word is the proper name “Gad.” It identifies Gad as a person and also appears in references connected with his tribal descendants and their inheritance. The name occurs 72 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Ezekiel. Because it functions as a name rather than a common descriptive term, its basic meaning in a sentence is the person, tribe, or territorial designation called Gad; the surrounding passage determines which is intended.

word:hebrew:H1429.explanation: Gediya means a young female goat, or kid.

policy.futureRepairGate: Reopen only after a verified source-alignment, lexical-identity, or evidence-view correction materially changes the closed evidence.
policy.priorReviewerNotes: The lexical evidence supports both senses, but Job 20:25 directly supports only “body,” not “back.” The single combined claim therefore is not fully Scripture-supported and is not atomic.

word:hebrew:H1601.explanation: Goah is a proper name for a location mentioned in the Hebrew Old Testament. It occurs only once, in Jeremiah 31:39, so its ordinary meaning is identifying that place rather than describing an action, quality, or person. The available rendering gives the name “Goah.” Without the verse text or a fuller lexical definition, Scripture here supports recognizing it as a place-name, while the surrounding passage supplies its specific significance.

word:hebrew:H1696.explanation: Dabar means to speak. It can also describe giving a command or teaching others.

word:hebrew:H1708.explanation: This word refers to “Dabbesheth,” a proper name used for a geographical location. It is not presented here as an ordinary action, quality, or object word, but as a name identifying a place. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:11. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, the name’s specific location and role in that passage cannot be explained further from this record alone.

word:hebrew:H1744.explanation: The word refers to a hoopoe, also rendered “lapwing,” a particular bird named in the Hebrew Old Testament. It is a noun naming the bird itself, rather than describing an action or quality. This Hebrew word occurs twice in the Old Testament corpus, once in Leviticus and once in Deuteronomy. The two approved renderings show that English translations may use different bird names for the same word. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse context.

word:hebrew:H1876.explanation: Dashah means to sprout or spring up.

word:hebrew:H1942.explanation: Havvah means ruin or calamity. It can also describe wickedness or mischief.

word:hebrew:H2002.explanation: Hamnîyk means a necklace or chain.

word:hebrew:H2183.explanation: Zânûwn means adultery and can figuratively mean idolatry. It describes sexual unfaithfulness and can also portray turning to idols.

word:hebrew:H2213.explanation: This Hebrew word means “crown.” It names a crafted crown or raised border associated with sacred furnishings in Exodus. Its use describes a feature made around or upon objects such as the ark and altar furnishings, rather than a person wearing a crown. The word occurs ten times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Exodus, where it consistently identifies this ornamental structural feature. word:hebrew:H2309.explanation: Chedel means rest, specifically the state of the dead.

word:hebrew:H2330.explanation: Chuwd means to put forth a riddle.

word:hebrew:H2345.explanation: This Hebrew word describes something brown in color. It appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Genesis 30, where it identifies the coloring of animals. The consistent rendering “brown” supports a straightforward color description rather than an action, title, or abstract idea. Its normal function is therefore to distinguish animals by their visible brown coloring. The surrounding verse determines the exact animal or wording being described in each occurrence.

word:hebrew:H2406.explanation: Chittah means wheat. It can refer to the wheat plant or to its grain used for flour.

word:hebrew:H242.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to “Sheerah,” a personal name rather than a common descriptive term. It appears twice in the Hebrew corpus, both times associated with 1 Chronicles 7:24. The available rendering identifies the word as a name, while the lexical record does not provide an additional gloss or short definition. Its role is therefore chiefly to identify this person; the surrounding verse supplies the specific information about her and her place in the passage.

word:hebrew:H2491.explanation: Chalal means pierced or wounded, especially to death.

word:hebrew:H2543.explanation: Chamowr means a male donkey, or ass.

word:hebrew:H2617.explanation: Cheçed means kindness, mercy, or loving-kindness. Scripture uses it for Yahweh’s mercy and loving-kindness, and for kindness shown by one person to another.

word:hebrew:H2734.explanation: Charah means to blaze up with anger, portraying anger as growing hot. It describes Cain as wroth and Yahweh’s anger as kindled.

word:hebrew:H2778.explanation: Charaph means to defy or reproach.

word:hebrew:H2792.explanation: Heresh is a personal name, rendered as “Heresh.” It identifies an individual mentioned once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 9:15. Because this word functions as a name rather than a common description, its basic meaning is the person it designates, not an action, quality, or theological concept. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain that individual’s role or setting; the name itself does not provide those details.

word:hebrew:H2837.explanation: This Hebrew word means “pleasure,” referring to something that brings satisfaction or is valued. It is used four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in passages from Kings, Chronicles, and Isaiah. The word names what is pleasing or wanted, while the surrounding sentence determines its particular use. Its central idea remains pleasure: something regarded with favor and sought with desire.

word:hebrew:H2895.explanation: Towb means to be good or well. It can also describe doing something well; Yahweh says Jehu did well by doing what was right.

word:hebrew:H2972.explanation: This Hebrew word means “Jairite.” It functions as a descriptive name, identifying a person by association with Jair. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 20:26. The available wording presents it as a personal or family designation rather than a general action, quality, or object. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the identity of the person being described.

word:hebrew:H2998.explanation: Jibnijah is the personal name of an Israelite.

word:hebrew:H3041.explanation: Jedidiah is a name for Solomon.

word:hebrew:H3104.explanation: The Hebrew word means “jubile,” functioning as a noun that names the Jubilee observance in the Old Testament. It occurs 27 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Leviticus, where the Jubilee is repeatedly discussed. The word also appears in passages connected with giving, including Leviticus 27:23. Its broader force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains the Jubilee itself rather than a general idea of celebration.

word:hebrew:H3148.explanation: Yowther means more or over and above. It can also express what is better or refer to profit.

word:hebrew:H3225.explanation: Yamin means the right hand or right side.

word:hebrew:H3250.explanation: Yiççôwr means a reprover, one who instructs.

word:hebrew:H3269.explanation: Jaazijah is the name of an Israelite, and English translations render it Jaaziah.

word:hebrew:H3287.explanation: Ya'eph means fatigued or exhausted, describing a person who is faint or weary.

word:hebrew:H3333.explanation: Yetsuqah means poured out or cast, referring to material run into a mold.

word:hebrew:H3452.explanation: Yeshimon means a desolation. It refers to a desert or wilderness, conveying the idea of a desolate land.

word:hebrew:H3539.explanation: Kadkod means a sparkling gem, probably a ruby. It can also refer to agate.

word:hebrew:H3575.explanation: Cuth or Cuthah names a province of Assyria.

word:hebrew:H3647.explanation: Kamas means to store away, or lay something up in store.

word:hebrew:H3690.explanation: Kislah can mean confidence or trust. It can also mean folly.

word:hebrew:H3746.explanation: This Hebrew noun refers to “captains,” identifying people who hold a recognized leadership position. It occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing once in 2 Samuel and twice in 2 Kings. The word functions as a designation for persons serving in an organized leadership role, rather than describing an action or quality. Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage and the responsibilities assigned to those called captains.

word:hebrew:H376.explanation: ʼÎysh means a man as an individual or a male person. In phrases such as “each man,” it can refer to each individual in a group, and it can also refer to a person.

word:hebrew:H3805.explanation: Kôthereth means the capital of a column, also called a chapiter.

word:hebrew:H3849.explanation: Log means a measure for liquids. Here it is a measure of oil.

word:hebrew:H3870.explanation: Luz is a place-name used for two places.

word:hebrew:H3953.explanation: Laqash means to gather the after crop.

word:hebrew:H4039.explanation: Megillah means a roll. It can also refer to a volume.

word:hebrew:H4075.explanation: This Hebrew word means “Mede,” identifying a person associated with the Medes. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Daniel 11:1. Here it functions as a concise identifying label. Because the available passage information does not include the verse text, the word’s specific role in that sentence should be understood from the surrounding context rather than from the name alone. Its basic sense is a national or people-group designation: a Mede.

word:hebrew:H4152.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to something connected with the death-related situation described in Joshua 20:9. It occurs only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its ordinary meaning cannot be established from repeated biblical usage. In its recorded setting, it functions as an object associated with dying, standing, and being struck, within the passage’s discussion of death. Its precise sense therefore depends especially on the wording and context of Joshua 20:9 rather than on a broader pattern of occurrences. [evidence_ids]

word:hebrew:H4246.explanation: Mecholah means a dance or dancing. It can describe people dancing together with tambourines.

word:hebrew:H426.explanation: Elah means God or god. It can refer to the God of heaven and earth. It is also used of gods that did not make the heavens and earth.

word:hebrew:H4390.explanation: Māle means to fill or be full. It describes water filling a valley and a person being filled with the Spirit of God.

word:hebrew:H4404.explanation: Malben means a brickkiln, a place associated with clay and mortar.

word:hebrew:H4448.explanation: Malal means to speak, say, or utter.

word:hebrew:H4541.explanation: Massekhah means a molten or cast image.

word:hebrew:H4633.explanation: Ma'arakh means an arrangement or preparation.

word:hebrew:H4725.explanation: Maqowm means a place, spot, or locality. It can identify a specific location chosen for people to come. It can also refer to a place where someone may flee.

word:hebrew:H4750.explanation: Miqshah means a cucumber patch or garden of cucumbers.

word:hebrew:H4769.explanation: Marbêts means a reclining place, especially a place where flocks lie down.

word:hebrew:H4787.explanation: Morrâh means trouble. It can also mean bitterness.

word:hebrew:H4893.explanation: Mishchath means disfigurement. It can also describe corruption or something marred.

word:hebrew:H4967.explanation: Methusael is a personal name in the Hebrew Old Testament, not a common word describing an object, action, or quality. It appears twice, both times in Genesis 4:18, within a genealogy. The name identifies a person who is presented as part of a family line through recorded births. Its precise significance as a name is not established here, so it is best understood simply as the person’s name.

word:hebrew:H4989.explanation: Mithcah is a Hebrew proper name, preserved in English as “Mithcah” or “Mithkah” rather than translated as an ordinary descriptive word. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Numbers 33:28–29. Since no explicit definition is provided, its meaning here is its identity as a named person or place in the biblical record, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what it designates. The two English spellings reflect pronunciation or spelling differences, not separate meanings.

word:hebrew:H5018.explanation: Nebuzaradan is the name of a Babylonian general.

word:hebrew:H5173.explanation: Nachash means enchantment—an incantation or augury.

word:hebrew:H5216.explanation: Nîyr means a lamp or light.

word:hebrew:H523.explanation: Ummah means a community of people and can also refer to a nation.

word:hebrew:H5281.explanation: Noʻŏmîy is the personal name Naomi.

word:hebrew:H5362.explanation: Naqaph means to go around or surround. It can also describe cutting.

word:hebrew:H5432.explanation: This Hebrew word means “measure.” It names a measure and refers to what determines extent or quantity. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 27:8. Its basic meaning is clear, while the surrounding verse is needed to identify exactly what is being measured and how the term functions in that sentence. The word therefore points to a standard or amount used for measuring, without itself describing an action or emotion.

word:hebrew:H5494.explanation: Sur means turned off or deteriorated, describing something degenerate.

word:hebrew:H5519.explanation: Sak means a crowd or multitude.

word:hebrew:H5520.explanation: Sok means a hut or shelter. It can also mean a lair or den.

word:hebrew:H5771.explanation: Avon means perversity or moral evil. It is commonly rendered “iniquity,” describing wrongdoing that can be carried or cleansed. It can also refer to punishment for iniquity, as in Cain’s statement that his punishment is greater than he can bear.

word:hebrew:H5803.explanation: Azgad is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Azgad.” It identifies a group or individual associated with the returning exiles and the community recorded after the exile. The name appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezra and Nehemiah, and is consistently treated as a proper name rather than translated as an ordinary descriptive word. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding passage, but its normal function is to identify the person or family called Azgad.

word:hebrew:H615.explanation: Asir means a captive or someone who is bound. It describes prisoners in custody and people bound with chains.

word:hebrew:H6176.explanation: Aroer means a juniper or juniper bush.

word:hebrew:H6327.explanation: Pûwts means to scatter or disperse. Scripture uses it for an army being scattered and for seed being scattered.

word:hebrew:H6385.explanation: Palag means to split or divide.

word:hebrew:H6415.explanation: This word refers to judgment—the act or result of deciding a matter rightly. It names a judicial determination rather than describing a person, place, or action by itself. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 16:3, so its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its basic sense points to a decision concerning what is right or how a matter should be settled.

word:hebrew:H6459.explanation: Peçel means an idol. It can also refer to a carved or graven image.

word:hebrew:H6460.explanation: Pesanterin means a lyre, also rendered psaltery.

policy.priorReviewerNotes: The lexical evidence supports both “rustic” and “village,” but the supplied Scripture evidence directly supports only the village sense. The single claim improperly combines two senses without direct Scripture support for “rustic.”

word:hebrew:H660.explanation: Eph'eh means an asp or other venomous serpent, such as a viper.

word:hebrew:H6626.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to an action associated with the grain offering in Leviticus 2:6, but its precise everyday meaning cannot be established from the available lexical information. It occurs only once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Leviticus 2:6. SEE relationships connect it with the offering and with other elements named in that verse, showing that it functions as part of the offering’s description. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its exact force there.

word:hebrew:H6723.explanation: Tsiyah means aridity—a condition of dryness.

word:hebrew:H6877.explanation: This Hebrew word means “high.” It functions as a descriptive term for something elevated or situated above the surrounding area. It appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in three verses, and its uses are connected with elevated places that people could occupy or use for refuge. The word’s basic sense remains focused on height rather than describing a person, action, or emotion. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

word:hebrew:H6899.explanation: Qibbuwts means a throng or company.

word:hebrew:H6914.explanation: Kibroth-hat-Taavah is the name of a place in the desert.

word:hebrew:H6958.explanation: Qow means to vomit or spew something out.

word:hebrew:H7067.explanation: Qanna means jealous. It describes Yahweh as a jealous God.

word:hebrew:H7089.explanation: This Hebrew word means “Destruction.” It names the state or outcome of being destroyed, expressing severe ruin rather than an ordinary difficulty or inconvenience. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, at Ezekiel 7:25. Because the available occurrence is a single appearance and no verse text is provided here, its precise force in that sentence belongs to the surrounding passage, while its basic meaning remains destruction.

word:hebrew:H7193.explanation: Qasqeseth means a fish scale and can also mean a coat of mail made of joined metal plates.

word:hebrew:H721.explanation: This Hebrew word identifies a person or people as an “Arvadite.” It functions as a group designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Genesis 10:18 and once in 1 Chronicles 1:16. The word’s normal sense is therefore an ethnic or family identification, while the surrounding verse supplies the particular role or setting in which the designation appears.

word:hebrew:H7236.explanation: Rebah means to grow. It can also describe making a man great.

word:hebrew:H7324.explanation: Rûwq means to pour out or empty.

word:hebrew:H7368.explanation: Rachaq means to become distant or be far away. It can also mean removing something, as when iniquity is put far away.

word:hebrew:H7382.explanation: Rêyach means smell. One passage says that the smell of fire was not on the men.

word:hebrew:H7405.explanation: This Hebrew verb means “bind”: to fasten or secure something by joining it firmly. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or abstract idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs only twice, both times in Exodus, showing a focused use rather than a broad range of applications. Its references are Exodus 28:28 and Exodus 39:21. The surrounding verse text would determine exactly what is being secured in each passage, but the word itself expresses the act of binding or fastening.

word:hebrew:H7449.explanation: Resen is a Hebrew proper name used for a place, not an ordinary descriptive word with a broader everyday meaning. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, and its English rendering is consistently “Resen.” Because no short definition or broader lexical gloss is provided, the safest understanding is simply the place-name itself. Its precise significance in Genesis 10:12 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are handled separately from this word-level meaning.

word:hebrew:H7470.explanation: Reuth means desire. It can also mean pleasure.

word:hebrew:H7553.explanation: Riqmah means variegated color. It can also refer to embroidered work.

word:hebrew:H7786.explanation: Sur means to rule or reign.

word:hebrew:H7852.explanation: Satam means to lurk for or persecute someone. It can also mean to hate or set oneself against someone.

word:hebrew:H79.explanation: The word means “wrestled,” describing an active physical struggle with another person. It functions as a verb, portraying someone engaged in sustained wrestling rather than simply speaking, disagreeing, or competing inwardly. This word occurs twice in the Old Testament, both in Genesis 32:24–25. Its repeated use in those two verses keeps the focus on the act of wrestling itself; the surrounding passage supplies the specific circumstances and significance of that struggle.

word:hebrew:H7900.explanation: Sok means a booth. It can also refer to a tabernacle.

word:hebrew:H7939.explanation: Sakar means payment or compensation, including wages or hire. It can also mean a reward received for service.

word:hebrew:H7975.explanation: Shiloach is a fountain in Jerusalem.

word:hebrew:H8017.explanation: Shelumiel is a personal name, referring to one particular man in Israel’s wilderness generation. It appears five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all within Numbers, from Numbers 1:6 through Numbers 10:19. The English translations preserve the name as “Shelumiel,” rather than translating it into an ordinary descriptive word. Because the available information identifies the person’s name but does not provide a lexical definition, its basic scriptural function is to identify him wherever he is mentioned. The surrounding verse is needed to explain his specific role in each occurrence.

word:hebrew:H8134.explanation: Shinab is a Hebrew personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Genesis 14:2, and is rendered “Shinab.” Because it functions as a name, its meaning is primarily identifying: it distinguishes one person from others mentioned in the biblical account. The surrounding verse and passage provide the details about that person, while the name itself does not describe a general concept.

word:hebrew:H8192.explanation: Shaphah means to abrade or make bare. It can also describe something sticking out.

word:hebrew:H8206.explanation: Shuppim is a Hebrew name rendered “Shuppim,” rather than an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears three times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, all in 1 Chronicles: 7:12, 7:15, and 26:16. The available passages identify it by name, but the verse text is not included here, so its precise family or historical role must be understood from those surrounding passages. Its function is chiefly to identify a named biblical figure or group.

word:hebrew:H8291.explanation: This Hebrew word describes something as “principal.” It functions as a descriptive term, identifying something by its primary status rather than expressing an action. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Isaiah 16:8. Because the available occurrence is isolated and no surrounding verse text is provided here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the sentence and wider context. Its basic lexical sense remains “principal,” referring to something regarded as having the leading place.

word:hebrew:H8343.explanation: Shashai is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, in Ezra 10:40, and English translations retain it as “Shashai.” Because the available passage information does not include the verse text or a defined lexical meaning, the name itself is the clearest supported sense. Its significance in that passage must be understood from the surrounding account.

word:hebrew:H8413.explanation: Tidal is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Tidal,” rather than an ordinary word describing an action or quality. It identifies a named person in Genesis 14, appearing twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Genesis 14:1 and 14:9. No explicit definition is given for the name, so its meaning here is its identifying function: Tidal names a person. Its significance in either verse must be understood from the surrounding passage, not from a separate word-definition.

word:hebrew:H8509.explanation: This Hebrew noun refers to a garment—something worn as clothing, rendered “garment” in its one Old Testament occurrence. It names an article of clothing rather than an action, quality, or person. The word appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Esther 8:15. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is a garment or robe worn by someone.

word:hebrew:H8530.explanation: Talpiyah describes something tall or slender. It can also mean an armoury.

word:hebrew:H8545.explanation: Temurah means an exchange or barter. It can also refer to restitution.

word:hebrew:H8602.explanation: Taphal means plaster and can also describe something untempered or unsavoury. Figuratively, it can describe foolish things.

word:hebrew:H884.explanation: Beer-Sheba is the name of a city.

word:hebrew:H956.explanation: This rare Hebrew word is connected with a “night” that has “passed.” It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Daniel 6:18, and describes the passing of a night rather than naming a person, object, or enduring quality. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding Hebrew sentence, but its recorded sense centers on the night and its passing. This helps readers recognize it as a time-related expression with a completed action.

word:hebrew:H97.explanation: This word refers to “Eglaim,” a proper place-name rather than an ordinary descriptive term. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 15:8. Because the available wording preserves the name itself and does not provide a descriptive definition, its basic meaning is the identification of that place. The precise significance of Eglaim in Isaiah depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.
